A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, Idiosyncrasies in Large Language Models. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices A–C support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original source-classification experiments, controlled transformations, synthetic-data fine-tuning experiments, model-similarity results, and supplementary analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds an alternative-rewriter analysis in Appendix B.5 and a ten-way classification result in Section 6.

M1.justification: The LLM2vec classifier, classification head, LoRA fine-tuning, TF-IDF analysis, and language-analysis procedures remain unchanged. The expanded main-text description of LoRA and 512-token truncation repeats information already in v1 Appendix A.2. The alternative rewriter is a robustness condition.

E1.justification: UltraChat, FineWeb, Cosmopedia, LmsysChat, WildChat, and the represented source-model families are retained. The ten-way experiment combines already studied source models. Non-Transformer models and unknown source-model sets are discussed as future work, without evaluations.

E2.justification: Table 6 retains ELMo, BERT, T5, and GPT-2 as comparisons with LLM2vec. The TF-IDF logistic-regression analysis also remains. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct is added as an alternative rewriting condition, not as a competing source-attribution method.

E3.justification: v2 adds a Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct rewriting condition and a pooled ten-class attribution experiment. The existing training recipe remains unchanged. The cross-dataset description changes from evaluating all four datasets to the other three, although Table 3 retains the same full matrix; this does not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Appendix B.5 tests sensitivity to the rewriting model by comparing paraphrasing, translation, and summarization using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and GPT-4o-mini. Existing prompt interventions, shuffling, markdown analyses, judge ablations, confusion matrices, and response examples are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports classifier seed counts, repeated-training uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The use of 35 response pairs for open-ended judge analysis is unchanged.

E6.justification: Tables 1–10 retain their numerical entries. New Table 12 reports Qwen rewriting accuracies of 92.6/94.3/71.5 and GPT-4o-mini accuracies of 93.6/93.9/63.7 for paraphrasing/translation/summarization. The latter differ without explanation from Table 10's retained chat scores of 91.4/91.8/58.1. Section 6 adds 92.2% ten-way accuracy. Section 2.2 also changes the attribution of the 40.3% small-training-set result from instruct LLMs to chat APIs, consistent with Figure 3.

T1.justification: The formal N-way classification setup and reasoning about chance accuracy under identical output distributions remain unchanged. No theorems, proofs, or substantive mathematical derivations are added.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add robust LLM evaluation as an implication, specifically vulnerability to manipulation of voting-based leaderboards. The central claims about source distinguishability, lexical and semantic idiosyncrasies, synthetic-data inheritance, and model similarity remain.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands the discussion beyond v1's synthetic-data and model-similarity implications. It adds leaderboard-manipulation risks and explicit applicability limits involving non-Transformer models, large or unknown source sets, and unresolved training mechanisms. It also clarifies that distinctive training-data effects are not exclusive to synthetic data and that paraphrasing can preserve formatting (Sections 4 and 6; Appendix C).

D1.justification: v2 explicitly documents shared train/validation splits across source models and exclusion of the 20 most frequent words when selecting characteristic phrases. Conversely, Table 7 loses its explanation of BERTScore rescaling against a human baseline. The detailed training recipe and code-access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Research positioning expands substantially through a new subsection on machine-generated text characteristics, including stylometry and human editing, plus additional authorship-attribution, training-fingerprint, API-auditing, and leaderboard-manipulation literature. Examples include Antoun, Chakrabarty, Suzuki, Cai, and Huang. The Jawahar survey and Zhang BERTScore references are removed.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized prose corrections, expands the classifier explanation before Section 2.1, and adds discussion, future-work, impact-statement, and appendix passages. The main section sequence and appendix organization remain largely intact; this is not an extensive rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds Table 12, reflows several existing figures and tables, renumbers response-example tables, and standardizes the frequency-axis scales in Figures 8 and 16. The remaining graphical content and response examples are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 improves the paper's framing through explicit applicability limits and broader research context, and adds a useful check of sensitivity to the rewriting model while preserving the central evidence. These gains are limited by the unexplained GPT-4o-mini score discrepancy between Tables 10 and 12 and removal of the BERTScore rescaling detail, which weaken reporting clarity and reproducibility.
